case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act requires a district court to stay a lawsuit pending arbitration when a party requests a stay, or whether the court has discretion to dismiss the case outright when all claims are referred to arbitration.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. §§ 1 et seq., specifically Section 3, which governs the staying of proceedings pending arbitration
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Wendy Smith et al.) argue that Section 3 of the FAA mandates a stay of proceedings when a party requests one, meaning district courts lack discretion to dismiss a case outright even when all claims are sent to arbitration; the statutory text of Section 3 is obligatory and does not confer judicial discretion to substitute dismissal for a stay
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Keith Spizzirri et al.) defend the Ninth Circuit's ruling, arguing that district courts retain discretionary authority to dismiss rather than stay proceedings when it is clear that the entire controversy between the parties will be resolved through arbitration, relying on a judicially-created exception to Section 3's stay requirement

Gilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp., 500 U.S. 20 (1991)

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference is in remarkable unanimity, and I find the core textual argument compelling: Section 3's 'shall stay' is mandatory language that admits no judicial discretion to substitute dismissal. Justice Kagan's citation of Lexecon, Inc. v. Milberg Weiss is particularly apt — we have consistently held that 'shall' creates obligations 'impervious to judicial discretion,' and I see no principled basis for treating Section 3 differently. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward the narrowest possible holding: courts must stay proceedings when a party requests it under Section 3, full stop — we need not resolve every ancillary question about inherent authority or the precise scope of supervisory jurisdiction. Justice Barrett's observation about the section heading 'Stay of Proceedings' and the structural coherence arguments from Justice Sotomayor regarding Sections 9-11 further reinforce that Congress designed a system premised on retained jurisdiction, making the Ninth Circuit's dismissal exception textually and structurally indefensible.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which is itself telling — when textualists and purposivists alike converge on the same reading, the statutory text is doing real work. Justice Barrett's point about the section heading 'Stay of Proceedings' is particularly apt from an originalist standpoint: the 1925 Congress titled the provision to signal its function, and that contemporaneous drafting choice confirms the mandatory stay interpretation. The strongest argument for respondents would be that courts possess inherent authority to manage their dockets, including through dismissal when all claims are arbitrable, but this argument fails under my methodology because inherent judicial authority cannot override an explicit statutory command — as I have consistently held, when Congress speaks clearly, courts must follow the text rather than resort to background principles of judicial administration. The word 'shall' in § 3 is not ambiguous, and the Ninth Circuit's discretion-to-dismiss exception is precisely the kind of atextual judicial improvisation that I condemned in Epic Systems, substituting a court's policy preferences for Congress's unambiguous mandate.

The strongest argument for respondents would be that inherent judicial authority permits dismissal when all claims are arbitrable and retention of jurisdiction serves no purpose, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, inherent authority cannot override an explicit statutory mandate — and the FAA's Sections 9-11 demonstrate that retention of jurisdiction always serves a purpose by providing an efficient forum for award confirmation, vacatur, or modification without requiring parties to re-file. The Ninth Circuit's judicially-created exception is precisely the kind of atextual gap-filling that this Court's FAA jurisprudence, from Epic Systems forward, has consistently and rightly rejected.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas and I reach the same conclusion through our respective methodologies, the statutory text is doing real work. Justice Kagan's invocation of Lexecon's holding that 'shall' creates an obligation 'impervious to judicial discretion' is particularly apt here, and Justice Jackson's point about how dismissal strips courts of supervisory authority resonates deeply with my concern for vulnerable litigants who need that judicial backstop when arbitration goes wrong. The strongest argument for respondents would be that dismissal is functionally equivalent to a stay and promotes judicial efficiency by clearing dockets — but this argument fails because Congress made the choice for us when it wrote 'shall stay,' and functional equivalence cannot override a clear statutory command, especially when dismissal actually harms parties by eliminating efficient pathways to confirm or vacate awards under Sections 9-11 without re-filing. The real-world consequences of dismissal fall disproportionately on workers and consumers who lack resources to navigate unnecessary procedural hurdles, which reinforces rather than undermines the textual conclusion that Congress got this right in 1925.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: My colleagues have converged on the same textual foundation I identified, and I find the unanimity here reflects genuine statutory clarity rather than groupthink — 'shall' in Section 3 simply does not leave room for a judicially-created dismissal option when a party requests a stay. Justice Sotomayor's emphasis on the practical harms to vulnerable litigants resonates with my pragmatic approach: dismissal doesn't just violate the text, it produces worse real-world outcomes by stripping courts of supervisory jurisdiction and burdening parties who need to return to court to enforce or challenge awards under Sections 9-11. Justice Jackson's structural point about Section 16 appellate rights is particularly sharp — permitting dismissal would effectively extinguish interlocutory appeal rights that Congress deliberately calibrated, which is a structural incoherence no court should countenance. The strongest counterargument for respondents would be inherent judicial authority or the notion that dismissal is functionally equivalent to a stay, but as I've noted, courts cannot invoke inherent authority to override an explicit statutory command, and 'functionally equivalent' is not the standard — Congress's actual text is.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 9 U.S.C. § 3 is unambiguous: when a party requests a stay, the court 'shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had.' Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Section 3 of the FAA is unambiguous: when a party requests a stay pending arbitration, the court 'shall' stay the proceeding — 'shall' being a mandatory directive under well-established principles of statutory interpretation, not a permissive grant of discretion.
